## Acts 10:1-24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Cornelius the Centurion

- **Cornelius** was a Roman centurion stationed at **Caesarea Maritima**, the Roman administrative capital of Judea, about 30 miles north of Joppa. He commanded about 100 men in the "Italian Regiment" (Cohors II Italica Civium Romanorum), a cohort of auxiliary troops drawn from Italy, considered among the most loyal Roman soldiers. (Enduring Word; Precept Austin; Pulpit Commentary)
- Centurions in the NT are consistently portrayed favorably — they were chosen for steadiness, character, and leadership, not just daring (Polybius). They were well-paid and held in high social esteem. (Precept Austin)
- **NET Bible note**: The Italian Cohort has been identified as *cohors II Italica*, known to have been stationed in Syria by AD 88. (Precept Austin)
- **Ellicott**: Luke may have learned these details from Philip the Evangelist during his stay at Caesarea (Acts 21:8) or possibly from Cornelius himself. Cornelius's admission "became, through its supernatural accompaniments… the ruling case on the subject" of Gentile inclusion. (Ellicott)

### v. 2 — A Devout God-Fearer

- **"Devout and God-fearing"**: Cornelius was what Jews called a "God-fearer" — a Gentile who worshipped the God of Israel, was sympathetic to Judaism, but stopped short of full conversion (circumcision and full observance). He was not a proselyte. (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary; Catholic Encyclopedia)
- The description shows he had regard to both tables of the law — piety toward God and love toward neighbor (alms to "the people," i.e., the Jewish people). (Gill)
- **Catholic Encyclopedia**: Cornelius was "one of those gentiles commonly, though incorrectly, called proselytes of the gate, who worshipped the one true God and observed some of the prescriptions of the Mosaic Law, but who were not affiliated to the Jewish community by circumcision." (Catholic Encyclopedia)
- **Gill** (Baptist/older): Cornelius was already a regenerate believer: "he was truly a gracious man, a converted person… his faith was of the same kind with that of the saints before the coming of Christ." Gill argues Cornelius already had saving faith but did not yet know that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah. (Gill)
- **Haydock's Catholic Commentary** (citing Augustine): "His former goodness could no longer avail him, unless he were, by the bond of Christian society and peace, incorporated with the Church; he is therefore ordered to send unto Peter." His alms and prayers were "acceptable preparatives for the grace of justification, and such as move God to mercy." (Haydock, from search excerpt)
- **Chrysostom** (Patristic/Orthodox): Marvels that a man of such wealth and power was so devout — "it is more wonderful when a person being in a position of wealth and power is such as these were." He was "careful of his soldiers also." (Chrysostom, Homily 22)
- **Matthew Henry**: Marks this as the great turning point in Acts — "now, 'Lo, we turn to the Gentiles;' and to them the door of faith is here opened: good news indeed to us sinners of the Gentiles." (Matthew Henry, from search excerpt)

### v. 3 — The Vision at the Ninth Hour

- The **ninth hour** (3:00 p.m.) was one of the three appointed Jewish hours of prayer. Cornelius confirms in Acts 10:30 that he was praying. The vision came while he was at prayer. (Enduring Word; Gill; Pulpit Commentary)
- **"Clearly" (φανερῶς)**: The adverb distinguishes this from a dream or trance — Cornelius was fully awake, eyes open, and the vision was distinct and unmistakable. (Ellicott; Gill; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Chrysostom**: Notes the timing — "at the ninth hour, when he was released from his cares and was at quiet, when he was engaged in prayers and compunction." (Chrysostom, Homily 22)

### v. 4 — "Your Prayers and Alms as a Memorial"

- **"Stared… in fear"**: Cornelius reacted with reverent fear (ἔμφοβος), a common response to angelic appearances among the godly in Scripture. The fear roused his attention; the angel's praise then mitigated the terror. (Enduring Word; Gill; Chrysostom)
- **"Memorial offering before God"**: The language evokes the sacrificial system — prayers and alms ascend like the smoke of a sacrifice on the altar, coming up for remembrance before God. The Pulpit Commentary says Cornelius's good works "were the fruit of his faith in God as revealed in the Old Testament." (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word; Gill)
- **Haydock** (Catholic, citing Chrysostom): "Nothing is more efficacious than the alms of a man, whose hands have not been defiled by injustice. It is a clear stream… It is a fountain springing to eternal life." (Haydock, search excerpt)

### vv. 5-6 — "Send for Simon Called Peter"

- God used an angel to direct Cornelius, but used a **man** (Peter) to preach the gospel. "Angels may help to connect men with God's appointed preachers, they are never allowed to do more" (Lenski). (Enduring Word)
- **Simon the tanner's house by the sea**: Tanners were considered ritually unclean by strict Jews because they handled dead animals. Peter's stay there already suggests his heart was being loosened from strict ceremonial scruples. Gill notes Jewish law required tanneries to be at least 50 cubits outside the city, usually on the east side (except the west, due to the temple orientation). (Gill)
- The angel gives three identifying tokens: Simon, surnamed Peter; staying with Simon a tanner; house by the sea — so there could be no mistake. (Chrysostom, Homily 22)

### vv. 7-8 — Cornelius Obeys Immediately

- Cornelius sent **two household servants and a devout soldier** — three witnesses, sufficient under Jewish law (Deut. 17:6; 19:15). This also honored Peter by sending a delegation rather than a single messenger. (Enduring Word; Gill)
- The faith of Cornelius was contagious — his household and at least one soldier shared his devotion. Gill notes these three were themselves religious men, properly chosen for the errand. (Enduring Word; Gill)
- He "explained what had happened" — Cornelius gave a full account so the messengers could relay it accurately to Peter. (Gill; Pulpit Commentary)

### v. 9 — Peter on the Rooftop at Noon

- **The next day**: The messengers likely set out early morning from Caesarea; Joppa was about 30 miles away. They approached Joppa around noon (the sixth hour), another appointed time of Jewish prayer. (Gill; Pulpit Commentary; Precept Austin)
- Flat rooftops in the ancient Near East served as a place of retreat, prayer, and rest. Peter went up to pray at noon. (Enduring Word; Gill; Pulpit Commentary)
- God was orchestrating both ends simultaneously: "Two men are thirty miles apart… God within the shadows keeping watch above His own, sends the angel to Caesarea, and grants the ecstatic trance in Joppa. They were thus brought together" (G. Campbell Morgan). (Enduring Word)

### v. 10 — Hunger and a Trance

- Peter became **very hungry** (πρόσπεινος — a rare word, occurring only here in the NT). He may have been fasting until the hour of prayer, as Cornelius was (v. 30). (Pulpit Commentary; Gill)
- While the meal was being prepared, Peter fell into a **trance** (ἔκστασις) — a state in which external senses are suspended and God imparts revelation directly to the mind. This was different from Cornelius's waking vision. (Pulpit Commentary; Gill; Calvin)
- God used Peter's physical hunger as the entry point for the vision about food. (Enduring Word)

### vv. 11-12 — The Sheet from Heaven

- **Heaven opened**: Not a literal tearing (as at Jesus' baptism or Stephen's vision), but in the vision. A vessel "like a large sheet" (the Greek word can also mean a large sail) descended, bound at its four corners and let down to earth. (Enduring Word; Gill; Ligonier/Sproul)
- **All kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles, and birds**: Both clean and unclean animals according to Leviticus 11 were mingled together. "The distinction between clean and unclean was very sharply drawn in the Levitical Law" (Pulpit Commentary). Peter would have been startled to see them all together. (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary; Gill)

### vv. 13-14 — "Kill and Eat!" / "No, Lord!"

- The command directly confronted Peter's lifelong commitment to kosher laws. Peter had "never eaten anything common or unclean" — a striking testimony to his conscientious Jewish piety even as a poor Galilean fisherman. (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word)
- **"No, Lord!"** — Enduring Word calls this "both absurd and yet typical of us. He said 'no' to his Lord. The only legitimate answer to a request from our Lord is 'yes.'" Peter had a habit of telling Jesus "no" (Matt 16:22; John 13:8). (Enduring Word)
- **R.C. Sproul** (Reformed): Peter was saying, "I've been a Jew since my birth… I have kept kosher, never had a piece of bacon… I have never broken the dietary laws in my entire life, and I'm not going to start now." The vision was the moment "centuries of dietary law and legal requirements God had sent to His people through Moses were instantly repealed, abrogated, and set aside." (Ligonier/Sproul)
- Chrysostom notes that even the apostles did not yet know the ceremonial law was to be abolished — they were only ignorant of the *timing*. The conversion of Cornelius was designed "to convince the Jews, rather than the apostles, that those ceremonies were no longer obligatory." (Haydock, citing Chrysostom)

### v. 15 — "What God Has Cleansed, Do Not Call Common"

- **Three times** the exchange occurred, for emphasis and certainty (cf. Gen 41:32). The repetition ensured Peter could not dismiss it as a momentary aberration. (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary; Gill)
- **Calvin**: "He speaketh of meats; but this sentence must be extended unto all parts of the life… It is not for us to allow or condemn any thing; but as we stand and fall by the judgment of God alone, so is he judge of all things." Calvin extends this to condemn later traditions that created new distinctions of foods (Montanists, the "Pope… made a law concerning meats"). (Calvin via CCEL)
- **Gill**: Notes that even rabbinic tradition acknowledged that in the Messianic age, unclean animals would be made clean again as they were for the sons of Noah (Gen 9:3). (Gill)
- **Sproul** (Reformed): Emphasizes that this was not ultimately about food — "it was about people. The rest of the chapter shows us the reason God repealed the dietary laws: those who were unclean were now being gathered together and made clean by Christ." (Ligonier/Sproul)

### v. 16 — Three Times, Then Taken Up

- The threefold repetition (cf. Peter's threefold denial and threefold restoration in John 21) gave solemn certitude. "By the time the drama had been acted out the third time, Peter must have begun to get the idea that God was trying to tell him something" (Boice). (Enduring Word)
- The sheet was "taken back up into heaven," indicating the vision's divine origin and the ratification of its message in heaven. Gill sees it also as picturing the church ultimately gathered up to heaven. (Enduring Word; Gill)

### vv. 17-18 — Peter Perplexed; The Messengers Arrive

- Peter was "puzzling over the meaning" — the vision did not come with immediate full understanding. God reveals progressively, and the interpretation arrived through providence: the knock at the gate. (Enduring Word; Gill)
- The messengers "made inquiry for Simon's house" — they had to ask around Joppa to find the tanner's house by the sea. (Gill; Pulpit Commentary)

### vv. 19-20 — The Spirit's Direct Instruction

- The **Holy Spirit** spoke to Peter, saying "I have sent them." This explicitly attributes the orchestration of both visions to the Spirit's direct agency — a clear mark of the Spirit's personality (cf. Acts 8:29; 13:2; 20:28). (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word)
- **"Without hesitation"** (nothing doubting): The command addressed Peter's inward perplexity directly. "For a time he was to walk, as it were, blindfold, but trusting in the full assurance of faith in the Hand that was guiding him" (Ellicott). (Ellicott)
- God did not yet tell Peter that the men were Gentiles. He simply said, "I have sent them" — enough for Peter to act in faith. (Enduring Word)

### v. 21 — Peter Greets the Messengers

- Peter went down and identified himself: "Here am I, the one you are looking for." He then asked their purpose — he still did not fully know why they had come. (Enduring Word)

### v. 22 — The Messengers Explain

- They describe Cornelius as **"a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation"** — an extraordinary commendation for a Roman officer among the people he was occupying. This recalls Luke 7:2-5, where Jewish elders similarly praised a centurion. (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word)
- Luke's "policy of conciliation" is evident: "all occasion of offence was, as far as possible, guarded against by the attestation given by those who were themselves Jews to the character of those concerned" (Ellicott). (Ellicott)
- The purpose: Cornelius was divinely instructed to **"hear a message from you"** — a Hebrew turn of phrase. Cornelius wanted to hear the gospel. (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word)

### v. 23 — Peter's Hospitality and Departure

- **"Peter invited them in as his guests"**: This was a radical breach of Jewish custom. "Normally a Jew would have said, 'Well, it is nice to meet you, but we need you to stay out here in the street'" (Boice). Peter not only let them in but **lodged** them (ἐξένισεν — "to entertain as a guest"; cf. Heb 13:2). Chrysostom says "He gave them friendly treatment, and made them at home with him." (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Enduring Word** (Pentecostal/Charismatic): Emphasizes that Peter's heart had genuinely changed through the vision even before he fully understood it. "By entertaining these Gentile guests, Peter went against the customs and traditions of Israel, but not against God's Word."
- Peter took **"some of the brothers from Joppa"** — six in number (Acts 11:12) — as witnesses, anticipating that what would happen in Caesarea would need verification before the Jerusalem church. (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott)
- The journey from Joppa to Caesarea was about 30 miles, normally two days' travel, stopping overnight halfway (likely at Apollonia on the coast road). (Pulpit Commentary)
- **Comparison with Jonah**: "Centuries ago another Jew had come to Joppa with a solemn message from his God… Jonah, the prophet, took a ship from Joppa and refused obedience to the divine call." Peter obeyed. (Gaebelein, cited by Enduring Word)

### v. 24 — Arrival at Caesarea

- **The following day** (the fourth day since Cornelius's vision), Peter arrived in Caesarea. The Pulpit Commentary calls this "a memorable event, being the first invasion of the Roman empire by the soldiers of the cross." (Pulpit Commentary)
- Cornelius was **expecting them** — a mark of his faith. He had never met Peter, knew only that he was a pious Jew who by tradition would have nothing to do with Gentiles, yet he trusted God to complete what He had begun. (Enduring Word)
- Cornelius had **"called together his relatives and close friends"** — an act of brotherly love and evangelistic zeal. Chrysostom suggests these were people Cornelius had already influenced toward the true God. This gathering became the first Gentile house-church congregation to hear the gospel. (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary; Chrysostom)
- **Catholic Encyclopedia**: "Cornelius became Bishop of Caesarea" (according to one tradition) or Bishop of Scepsis in Mysia (another tradition). (Catholic Encyclopedia)

## Traditions Compared

### On Whether Cornelius Was Already "Saved" Before Meeting Peter

This is the most significant theological difference among traditions on this passage:

- **Baptist / Older Evangelical (Gill)**: Cornelius was already regenerate, a true believer with saving faith in the coming Messiah — his faith was "of the same kind with that of the saints before the coming of Christ." He simply lacked knowledge that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah. (Gill)
- **Reformed (implied by Sproul)**: The vision was about God's sovereign inclusion of the elect from among the Gentiles. Cornelius's piety was genuine God-given preparation, but he still needed to hear the gospel of Jesus Christ and believe for salvation. Sproul emphasizes that the dietary laws were repealed so "those who were unclean were now being gathered together and made clean by Christ." (Ligonier/Sproul)
- **Catholic (Haydock; Augustine)**: Cornelius's good works were "acceptable preparatives for the grace of justification, and such as move God to mercy" — but they did not suffice for salvation before baptism and incorporation into the Church. As Augustine said, "His former goodness could no longer avail him, unless he were, by the bond of Christian society and peace, incorporated with the Church." (Haydock, search excerpts)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word)**: "Even Cornelius, a genuinely good and pious man, still needed to come to Jesus as Lord and Savior; goodness and God-fear are not substitutes for faith in Christ." The emphasis falls on the necessity of hearing and responding to the preached gospel, with the Spirit's outpouring as confirmation. (Enduring Word)

### On the Meaning of the Vision

- **Reformed (Sproul)**: The dietary laws were "instantly repealed, abrogated, and set aside" at this moment. The primary point was about people, not food — the inclusion of Gentiles cleansed by Christ. This is a redemptive-historical turning point. (Ligonier/Sproul)
- **Lutheran (implied by Calvin's citation of similar concerns)**: Calvin stresses that the principle extends beyond food to all of life: "It is not for us to allow or condemn any thing." He specifically applies it against later church traditions that imposed new food laws. Lutheran theology would similarly emphasize the abrogation of ceremonial law and Christian liberty. (Calvin via CCEL)
- **Catholic (Haydock)**: "God had not already sanctified the Gentiles; but he had called them, that they might become so. He had thrown down the wall of separation… Jesus Christ, by his blood, had generally reconciled all mankind to his Father." The vision teaches that all now "had a right to communicate in the truths of the gospel, and in the sacraments." (Haydock, search excerpts)

### On Peter's Role

- **Catholic**: Peter, as the chief apostle and first pope, is the one through whom the door to the Gentiles is opened. Cornelius must send for Peter specifically — not just any apostle. "He does not send him to some great one, but… He brings the chief Apostle (to these Gentiles)" (Chrysostom). (Chrysostom, Homily 22)
- **Protestant**: The emphasis falls on God's sovereignty in orchestrating both visions and the Spirit's direct command. Peter is the chosen instrument, but the focus is on what God is doing, not Petrine primacy. The Spirit says "I have sent them" — not Peter's authority but divine initiative is central. (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary)

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes; Bible Odyssey)

- **NET Bible**: Notes that the Italian Cohort "has been identified as cohors II Italica which is known to have been stationed in Syria in A.D. 88." The term "centurion" designates a noncommissioned officer commanding about 100 men; Roman troops in Judea were typically auxiliaries rewarded with citizenship after 25 years' service. (Precept Austin, citing NET)
- **Historical dating**: The event is placed around AD 38-41, about 5-10 years after Pentecost. "The tenth chapter of Acts is one of the most important chapters in Acts, perhaps also one of the most important chapters in the Bible" (Boice). (Precept Austin)

### Patristic (Chrysostom, via New Advent)

- **Chrysostom** emphasizes the divine condescension: "When Paul was to be brought over, there is no angel, but the Lord Himself: and He does not send him to some great one, but to a very ordinary person: but here, on the contrary, He brings the chief Apostle (to these Gentiles), not sends them to him: herein condescending to their weakness, and knowing how such persons need to be treated." (Chrysostom, Homily 22)
- He also highlights Cornelius's care for his whole household and his soldiers as a model for family religion. (Chrysostom, Homily 22)

### Catholic (Catholic Encyclopedia)

- The baptism of Cornelius "is an important event in the history of the Early Church. The gates of the Church, within which thus far only those who were circumcised and observed the Law of Moses had been admitted, were now thrown open to the uncircumcised Gentiles without the obligation of submitting to the Jewish ceremonial laws." This was initially controversial (Acts 11:2-3) but settled at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). (Catholic Encyclopedia)
